metadata.title: Do school resources reduce socioeconomic achievement gap? Evidence from PISA 2015

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 student microdata for 15-year-olds across 39 countries/economies and constructs an analytic dataset of 300,218 students. The authors explicitly follow OECD/PISA guidance by using the final student weight and 80 replicate weights to compute sampling-variance estimates, and they report that this approach is used to account for PISA’s complex survey design while analyzing plausible values. Missing values are imputed using country- or school-mean values for continuous variables and country- or school-median values for categorical variables, with an additional missingness indicator included in models. Because the analysis is implemented as fixed-effects regressions with clustered standard errors (not ML), the paper does not discuss any ML-specific weighting limitations; instead, it treats weights as required for unbiased PISA inference with plausible values.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PISA 2015 data for 15-year-old students in 39 participating countries/economies. They identify missing values and impute them with country- or school-mean values for continuous variables and with country- or school-median values for categorical variables. They exclude observations if its values are missing across all students within a school or all schools within a country. The final analytic dataset therefore includes 300,218 students with plausible-value-based mathematics, reading, and science outcomes and a set of student-, family-, and school-level covariates.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Fixed-effects regression with country fixed effects; clustered standard errors at school level. R-squared: 0.528 (computers model) and 0.528 (teachers model). Coefficients reported in Table 2 (e.g., computers per student: -0.332 (0.831); master degreed teachers: -0.587 (1.863)).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged computers per student, master degreed teachers, SES index, learning time, and private school to model mathematics achievement (plausible values), finding that neither material resources nor human resources show a statistically significant association with mathematics scores in the within-country fixed-effects specification. This indicates that, at least for mathematics, simply increasing school computers or the share of teachers with master’s degrees may not translate into measurable achievement gains once time-invariant country differences are controlled.

main_findings.target_variable: Heterogeneous effect: Mathematics achievement by SES (interaction)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3 (FE estimates with country fixed effects; clustered SE at school level). Interaction (computers × SES): 0.613 (0.923), not significant. Interaction (teachers × SES): 7.981 (1.558), p < 0.001. R-squared: 0.527 (computers) and 0.527 (teachers).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged computers per student, master degreed teachers, and SES index to model mathematics achievement heterogeneity via the school-resources × SES interaction, finding that the SES gradient is negligible for material resources but significantly positive for human resources (teachers × SES: 7.981, p < 0.001). This indicates that increasing teacher quality as proxied by master’s-degree shares may widen the socioeconomic achievement gap, because the marginal benefit grows with students’ SES.

main_findings.target_variable: Heterogeneous effect difference: OECD vs non-OECD (interaction)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 4 (FE with country fixed effects; clustered SE at school level). For teachers × SES in mathematics: School resources × SES index = 0.102 (1.660), not significant; OECD moderation term = 4.402 (2.450), not significant. For material resources in mathematics: School resources × SES index = -0.667 (0.609), not significant; OECD moderation = 1.478 (0.932), not significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged master degreed teachers, SES index, and OECD membership to test whether the SES-dependent human-resource effect differs between OECD and non-OECD countries for mathematics, finding that the SES gradient for human resources is not statistically significant and shows no clear OECD moderation. This indicates that the equity implications of teacher-quality proxies may be more pronounced in reading than in mathematics when comparing OECD and non-OECD contexts.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Fixed-effects regression with country fixed effects; clustered standard errors at school level. R-squared: 0.528 (computers model) and 0.528 (teachers model). Coefficients reported in Table 2 (e.g., computers per student: -0.730 (1.196); master degreed teachers: 1.346 (2.778)).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged computers per student, master degreed teachers, SES index, learning time, and private school to model reading achievement (plausible values), finding that neither material resources nor human resources show a statistically significant association with reading scores in the within-country fixed-effects specification. This indicates that resource expansion measured by computers per student and master’s-degree teacher shares may not improve reading outcomes on average after accounting for country fixed effects.

main_findings.target_variable: Heterogeneous effect: Reading achievement by SES (interaction)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3 (FE estimates with country fixed effects; clustered SE at school level). Interaction (computers × SES): 1.045 (0.899), not significant. Interaction (teachers × SES): 7.855 (1.615), p < 0.001. R-squared: 0.450 (computers) and 0.451 (teachers).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged computers per student, master degreed teachers, and SES index to model reading achievement heterogeneity via the school-resources × SES interaction, finding that material resources show no SES-dependent pattern while human resources show a significant positive SES interaction (teachers × SES: 7.855, p < 0.001). This indicates that policies increasing teacher qualifications may disproportionately benefit higher-SES students in reading, potentially worsening educational equity.

main_findings.target_variable: Heterogeneous effect difference: OECD vs non-OECD (interaction)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 4 (FE with country fixed effects; clustered SE at school level). For teachers × SES in reading: School resources × SES index = 5.610 (3.765), p < 0.05; additional OECD moderation term (teachers × SES × OECD) = -0.770 (2.669), not significant. For material resources in reading: School resources × SES index = 1.615 (0.984), not significant; OECD moderation = -0.807 (1.331), not significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged master degreed teachers, SES index, and OECD membership to test whether the SES-dependent human-resource effect differs between OECD and non-OECD countries, finding that the SES gradient for human resources remains statistically significant for reading but does not meaningfully change between OECD and non-OECD contexts (OECD moderation term not significant). This indicates that inequitable returns to teacher-quality proxies may be a cross-context pattern rather than an OECD-only phenomenon.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Fixed-effects regression with country fixed effects; clustered standard errors at school level. R-squared: 0.460 (computers model) and 0.460 (teachers model). Coefficients reported in Table 2 (e.g., computers per student: -0.792 (1.256); master degreed teachers: -0.234 (1.871)).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged computers per student, master degreed teachers, SES index, learning time, and private school to model science achievement (plausible values), finding that neither material resources nor human resources show a statistically significant association with science scores in the within-country fixed-effects specification. This indicates that, for science, these particular resource proxies may not be sufficient levers for improving achievement once unobserved time-invariant country factors are removed.

main_findings.target_variable: Heterogeneous effect: Science achievement by SES (interaction)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3 (FE estimates with country fixed effects; clustered SE at school level). Interaction (computers × SES): 1.013 (0.975), not significant. Interaction (teachers × SES): 11.372 (1.344), p < 0.001. R-squared: 0.470 (computers) and 0.471 (teachers).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged computers per student, master degreed teachers, and SES index to model science achievement heterogeneity via the school-resources × SES interaction, finding that material resources do not vary by SES but human resources do (teachers × SES: 11.372, p < 0.001). This indicates that teacher-quality improvements measured by advanced degrees may amplify socioeconomic disparities in science achievement.

main_findings.target_variable: Heterogeneous effect difference: OECD vs non-OECD (interaction)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 4 (FE with country fixed effects; clustered SE at school level). For teachers × SES in science: School resources × SES index = 2.776 (1.797), not significant; OECD moderation term = 4.542 (2.336), not significant. For material resources in science: School resources × SES index = 0.479 (0.668), not significant; OECD moderation = 0.427 (1.066), not significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged master degreed teachers, SES index, and OECD membership to test whether the SES-dependent human-resource effect differs between OECD and non-OECD countries for science, finding no statistically significant evidence of SES-dependent human-resource returns or OECD moderation. This indicates that the widening-gap concern tied to teacher-quality proxies may be weaker or less detectable for science in this OECD vs non-OECD comparison.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2015 microdata for 15-year-olds in 39 countries/economies (final analytic sample: 300,218 students) to examine whether school resources relate to achievement and whether those relationships differ by students’ socioeconomic status (SES) and OECD membership. Outcomes are mathematics, reading, and science plausible values (0–1000, mean 500, SD 100), and the authors use country fixed effects with standard errors clustered at the school level, applying PISA final student weights and 80 replicate weights and averaging across plausible values. In the average within-country models, neither computers per student nor the share of teachers with master’s degrees is significantly associated with achievement (R² around 0.46–0.53). However, human resources show significant positive interactions with SES (e.g., teachers × SES: 7.981 in math; 7.855 in reading; 11.372 in science, all p < 0.001), implying larger returns for higher-SES students and thus a widening socioeconomic achievement gap. The paper is cross-sectional and uses resource proxies, so causal claims are limited and measurement may not capture how resources are used.
